Riding Alongside Heritage Railways

There's something magical about riding a motorcycle alongside a working steam railway. The puff of smoke, the whistle echoing through a valley, the sense of two forms of transport from different eras sharing the same landscape. Britain has over 150 heritage railways, and many have parallel roads that create unique riding experiences.

The Great Ones

  • West Highland Line (Fort William to Mallaig): The road (A830, the Road to the Isles) runs parallel to the railway line used by the Jacobite steam train — the Harry Potter train crossing the Glenfinnan Viaduct. Time your ride to see the steam train crossing the viaduct (departs Fort William at 10:15am in season).
  • Ffestiniog Railway (Porthmadog to Blaenau Ffestiniog): The narrow-gauge railway winds through Snowdonia. The A487 and A496 roads offer parallel riding with views of the tiny trains climbing through the mountains.
  • Settle-Carlisle Railway: The B6259 and minor roads through the Yorkshire Dales run alongside this spectacular Victorian railway. Ribblehead Viaduct is the centrepiece — time your ride to see a train crossing the arches.
  • North York Moors Railway (Pickering to Whitby): The road through Newton Dale parallels the railway through deep, forested gorges. Steam trains operate regularly in the season.

Wales's Narrow Gauge Treasures

  • Snowdon Mountain Railway: The road to Pen-y-Pass runs close to the lower section. Watch the rack-and-pinion trains climbing Snowdon from the Llanberis Pass road.
  • Vale of Rheidol Railway (Aberystwyth to Devil's Bridge): The road parallels this narrow-gauge line through the beautiful Rheidol Valley. Both the ride and the railway are excellent.
  • Talyllyn Railway: One of the first preserved railways in the world. The road through the Fathew Valley alongside the railway is a quiet, beautiful ride.

Scotland

  • Strathspey Railway (Aviemore to Broomhill): Running through the Cairngorms alongside the River Spey. The B9153 gives views of the steam trains against a Highland backdrop.
  • Bo'ness & Kinneil Railway: On the Firth of Forth. A short railway but atmospheric, with views across the estuary.
Check railway timetables before your ride and time your arrival at key viewpoints to coincide with train departures. The combination of a steam locomotive and your motorcycle in the same landscape creates extraordinary photographic opportunities.

Photography Tips

  • Find an elevated viewpoint that shows both the railway and road in the same frame
  • Steam is most visible against dark backgrounds (hillsides, forests)
  • The Glenfinnan Viaduct viewpoint is crowded — arrive early and claim your spot
  • Video works well for steam trains — capture the motion and sound

Heritage railways and motorcycles share something fundamental — they're both about the joy of the journey, the romance of travel, and the celebration of engineering. faq.q: How do I time my ride to see the Jacobite on Glenfinnan Viaduct?
faq.a: The Jacobite steam train departs Fort William at around 10:15am in season, reaching Glenfinnan Viaduct roughly half an hour later. Ride the A830 in good time, arrive early at the viaduct viewpoint car park and claim your spot, because it gets very crowded. Always check current timetables on the operator's website, as departure times shift between seasons.

faq.q: Where should I stand to photograph a steam train and my bike together?
faq.a: Find an elevated viewpoint that shows both the railway and the road in the same frame, such as the hillside above Glenfinnan or the moor above Ribblehead. Steam shows up best against dark backgrounds like forested slopes or hillsides. Video works particularly well for steam because it captures the motion, whistle and sound as the locomotive passes.

faq.q: Do I need to book anything to ride these routes?
faq.a: No, the roads themselves are public and free to ride at any time. You only need to plan around the railway timetables if you want to see a train. Check each railway's website in advance, as most steam services run seasonally, often Easter to October, with reduced or no winter operation. Turning up on a non-running day means an empty line.

faq.q: Which railway route is best for a quiet ride?
faq.a: The Vale of Rheidol Railway road through the Rheidol Valley and the Talyllyn Railway road through the Fathew Valley are both quiet, beautiful and far less busy than Glenfinnan. They suit riders who want the atmosphere of steam without the crowds. The narrow-gauge trains are charming and the surrounding mid-Wales scenery is excellent throughout.
